title: Using hydrostatic pressure difference
prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 8 derived hydrostatic pressure difference from the weight of a static liquid column.
Students can explain why only the vertical depth difference matters for a fluid of uniform density.
Earlier work established SI units, density, pressure and the use of W = mg.
new_learning: Calculate pressure difference in a static fluid and rearrange the relationship to find density or depth difference.
Distinguish a pressure difference caused by a liquid column from the absolute pressure at one point.
Use differences or graph gradients so a common surface pressure cancels.

blocks.title: Two lakes, the same pair of depths
content: Two pressure sensors are 1.0 m apart vertically in a lake. A storm changes the air pressure above the whole lake. Will the pressure difference between the sensors change?

The pressure shown by each sensor may change, but the extra air pressure reaches both positions. The difference between them still comes from the weight of the 1.0 m liquid column between them. This is why pressure difference is often the shortest route through a hydrostatic problem.

figure.purpose: Create the opening prediction by separating a shared surface-pressure change from the liquid-column pressure difference.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison sketch of the same lake before and during a storm. Show two submerged sensors with a fixed 1.0 m vertical separation. Use equal added downward air-pressure arrows at the surface in the storm panel and keep all sensor readings hidden.
figure.alt_text: Two sensors keep the same vertical separation while surface air pressure changes equally above the lake.

blocks.title: The pressure-difference relationship
content: This is the formula to remember: Δp = ρgΔh. Here Δp is the pressure difference in pascals, ρ is the uniform fluid density in kilograms per cubic metre, g is the acceleration of free fall in metres per second squared, and Δh is the vertical depth difference in metres.

Choose the deeper point minus the shallower point. In a static liquid, pressure increases with depth, so this choice makes both Δp and Δh positive. If the order is reversed, both differences are negative and the same physics is preserved.
The formula uses vertical separation, not the distance along a sloping pipe or the length of a winding route through the liquid.

figure.purpose: Fix the meanings, units and consistent subtraction order in the hydrostatic formula.
figure.brief: Rectangular annotated teacher sketch of two points S and D in one static liquid. Mark D deeper than S, show vertical bracket Δh, label Δp as p_D minus p_S, and place a compact symbol-and-unit key beside the vessel.
figure.alt_text: A deeper point D and shallower point S define positive pressure and depth differences.

blocks.title: Difference is not the same as absolute pressure
content: The quantity ρgΔh is the change in pressure between two levels. It is not automatically the total or absolute pressure at the deeper point.

If the pressure at the upper point is known, the deeper pressure equals the upper pressure plus the hydrostatic pressure difference. If the upper point is the liquid surface, its pressure may be atmospheric pressure or another stated external pressure.

It can feel natural to put the deeper absolute pressure straight into Δp = ρgΔh because that is the largest pressure number in the question. That fails because Δp must compare two points. Subtract the two pressures first, then match that pressure difference to the depth difference between the same points.

figure.purpose: Contrast absolute pressure at one point with the pressure difference between two points.
figure.brief: Rectangular two-column teacher sketch. Left column shows a surface pressure contribution shared through the liquid. Right column shows the additional liquid-column contribution between upper point S and deeper point D. Include the word relationship deeper pressure equals upper pressure plus pressure difference, but no numerical answer.
figure.alt_text: The deeper absolute pressure contains both the upper-point pressure and an added hydrostatic difference.

blocks.title: From two depths to a pressure difference
content: A tank contains oil of density 850 kg m⁻³. One probe is 0.25 m below the surface and another is 1.45 m below the surface. The vertical depth difference is Δh = 1.45 m - 0.25 m = 1.20 m.

Use the remembered formula with the same subtraction order: Δp = ρgΔh = 850 kg m⁻³ × 9.81 m s⁻² × 1.20 m = 1.0006 × 10⁴ Pa. To three significant figures, the deeper probe is at a pressure 1.00 × 10⁴ Pa greater than the shallower probe.

Independent check: ρg is about 8500 Pa per metre, so a 1.2 m change should give about 10 000 Pa. The calculated size is sensible. The surface pressure was not needed because it would be common to both probe readings.

figure.purpose: Teach the subtraction of two depths before substitution and show a separate magnitude check.
figure.brief: Rectangular worked-layout sketch with an oil tank and probes at 0.25 m and 1.45 m. Beside it show four boxes: subtract depths, select Δp=ρgΔh, substitute with units, estimate 8500 Pa per metre times 1.2 m.
figure.alt_text: Two oil-probe depths are subtracted before calculating and estimating their pressure difference.

blocks.title: Use two pressure readings to find density
content: Two sensors in the same static liquid are at depths 0.35 m and 1.30 m. Their absolute readings are 104.6 kPa and 112.9 kPa. First match the differences: Δp = 112.9 kPa - 104.6 kPa = 8.3 kPa = 8300 Pa, and Δh = 1.30 m - 0.35 m = 0.95 m.
Rearrange before inserting values: ρ = Δp/(gΔh). Then ρ = 8300 Pa/(9.81 m s⁻² × 0.95 m) = 8.91 × 10² kg m⁻³, so the density is 890 kg m⁻³ to two significant figures.
A reverse check gives ρgΔh = 890 kg m⁻³ × 9.81 m s⁻² × 0.95 m = 8.29 × 10³ Pa, which returns the measured 8.3 kPa difference. The absolute readings were useful only through their difference.

figure.purpose: Model paired subtraction, rearrangement and reverse substitution when density is unknown.
figure.brief: Rectangular annotated calculation map. Pair 112.9 kPa with depth 1.30 m and 104.6 kPa with depth 0.35 m using matching colours. Arrows lead to Δp and Δh, then to ρ=Δp/(gΔh), then a reverse-check loop.
figure.alt_text: Matched pressure and depth differences lead to a density and a reverse check.

blocks.title: Find an unknown change in depth
content: A stationary seawater region has density 1030 kg m⁻³. The pressure increases by 44.5 kPa between two points. Convert first: Δp = 44.5 × 10³ Pa.
Rearrange for the vertical separation: Δh = Δp/(ρg) = 44.5 × 10³ Pa/(1030 kg m⁻³ × 9.81 m s⁻²) = 4.40 m.

The result is a change in depth, not the deeper point's depth below the surface. To find that absolute depth, the shallower depth would also be needed. A dimensional check gives Pa divided by Pa per metre, leaving metres.

figure.purpose: Separate a calculated depth difference from an absolute depth below the surface.
figure.brief: Rectangular three-level seawater sketch with surface, shallower point and deeper point. Mark only the bracket between the two points as unknown Δh. Put a question mark on the shallower point's surface depth to show why the deeper absolute depth cannot yet be found.
figure.alt_text: A pressure change determines the separation between two seawater points but not either absolute depth.

blocks.title: A graph makes the common pressure visible
content: For one uniform liquid, a graph of absolute pressure against depth is a straight line. Its gradient is Δp/Δh = ρg. The pressure-axis intercept is the pressure at zero liquid depth, usually the stated surface pressure.

Use this route: identify the two matching levels, subtract pressures in the same order as depths, convert kilopascals and centimetres when needed, rearrange Δp = ρgΔh, substitute with units, then check the sign, magnitude and meaning of the result.

A non-zero graph intercept does not change the gradient. This is the graphical version of the storm puzzle: a shared surface pressure moves the whole line up or down, while the pressure difference over a fixed depth and the gradient stay unchanged.

figure.purpose: Synthesize gradient, intercept and the difference-first calculation route.
figure.brief: Rectangular teacher sketch with two parallel absolute-pressure-against-depth lines for two surface pressures. Mark equal gradients ρg, different intercepts, and one identical Δp bracket over the same Δh. Add a short calculation checklist below.
figure.alt_text: Changing surface pressure shifts a pressure-depth line without changing its gradient or fixed-depth pressure difference.

concepts_taught: hydrostatic pressure difference between two levels
absolute pressure compared with pressure difference
misconceptions_addressed: The deeper absolute pressure can be substituted directly as Δp.
The length of a sloping route replaces the vertical depth difference.
A pressure difference gives an absolute depth without another reference depth.
A change in surface pressure changes the hydrostatic gradient.
skills_students_can_now_use: Use and rearrange Δp = ρgΔh to find pressure difference, density or vertical depth difference.
Subtract matching pressure and depth values in a consistent order.
Distinguish absolute pressure from a pressure difference.
Use a pressure-depth graph gradient to find density and its intercept to identify surface pressure.
